client: Lately, I’ve been really struggling to focus at work. Every time I try to get things done, I start thinking about my grandma, and it just hits me all over again how much I miss her. I’m not sure if talking about it will really help—it feels like nothing can change the fact that she’s gone.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of grief with you, and it’s understandable that those feelings make it hard to focus. Would it feel okay to explore how these thoughts about your grandma show up and how they might be influencing your day?

client: I guess I’m just stuck in this loop where I think about her all the time, and it makes me feel guilty—like I didn’t spend enough time with her when she was here. Sometimes I wonder if I’m just holding onto this pain because I feel like I deserve to feel bad about it. But I don’t know if talking about it will actually help me let go of that guilt.
therapist: That guilt sounds really heavy to carry—it makes sense that it would keep you stuck in this painful loop. What do you think your grandma might say if she could see how much love is behind this guilt you're feeling?

client: I don’t know… I guess she’d probably tell me not to be so hard on myself. She was always like that—so kind and forgiving. But it’s hard for me to accept that forgiveness now. Part of me feels like I don’t deserve it because I wasn’t there enough for her when she needed me. I don’t know how to let go of that.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding yourself to a standard that your grandma wouldn't have wanted for you—that's such an important insight. What would it feel like to try treating yourself with just a fraction of that kindness she showed others, even for a moment?

client: I don’t know if I can be kind to myself about this—it feels like I’m letting myself off the hook too easily. I keep thinking, “If I don’t hold onto this guilt, then I’m just ignoring what I did wrong.” It’s like punishing myself is the only way to make up for not being there for her.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become a way to stay connected to your grandma, almost like letting go would mean losing her all over again. How might it feel to explore other ways to honor her memory that don't involve punishing yourself?

client: That’s an interesting way to look at it—I never thought of guilt as a way to stay connected to her. But I don’t know how to honor her memory without feeling this weight. It’s hard to imagine doing something positive when I’m so focused on what I didn’t do for her. What if trying to honor her feels like pretending everything is okay when it’s not?
therapist: It makes sense that shifting away from guilt might feel like pretending—you're understandably holding space for both love and loss. What small act of remembrance might feel genuine to you, even if it's bittersweet?

client: Maybe writing her a letter or something—just to say the things I didn’t get to say. But I don’t know if that would help or just make me feel worse. What if it just brings up more sadness and I end up feeling even more stuck than I do now?
therapist: Writing to her could bring up sadness—and that's okay, because grief and love often travel together. What if we viewed the letter as a way to make space for both the pain and the love, rather than expecting it to "fix" anything right away?

client: I guess I could try writing a letter—but I’m worried I’ll just end up repeating the same thoughts over and over, like how I didn’t do enough for her. What if it doesn’t help me feel closer to her and just makes me feel worse about myself? I don’t know if I’m ready to face that.
therapist: It’s okay to feel hesitant—this is a deeply personal and emotional process, and it’s natural to worry about it bringing up more pain. How would it feel to start small, maybe jotting down just one memory or moment with her that made you feel close, and seeing where that takes you?

client: I guess I could try writing down one memory—maybe something small, like how she used to make my favorite cookies when I visited. But I’m worried that even thinking about those good times will just remind me of how I didn’t visit her enough. What if focusing on the happy memories makes me feel even more guilty for not being there more often?
therapist: That worry makes so much sense—it shows how much you cared, and how deeply you wish things had been different. What if we thought of these memories not as reminders of what you missed, but as proof of the love that was always there between you?

client: I guess I’ve never really thought of it that way—that these memories could be proof of the love between us instead of just reminders of what I didn’t do. But it’s hard to shift my thinking like that. What if focusing on the love just makes me feel even more sad that I didn’t show it enough when she was here?
therapist: Grief often brings these complicated layers—where love and sadness exist side by side without cancelling each other out. What would it feel like to acknowledge that the depth of your sadness now is also a reflection of how much you cared then?

client: I guess I never thought of it that way—that my sadness shows how much I cared. But it’s still hard to accept that I didn’t show it enough when she was here. It feels like the love I feel now doesn’t make up for the time I missed with her. I don’t know if focusing on that love will really help me feel better or just make me feel more regret.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding two truths at once—the love you shared was real, and the wish for more time together is also real. How might it feel to gently make space for both, without forcing one to outweigh the other?
